data.title: Gaius Iulius Caesar: the construction of Celtic hillforts and the capture of Avaricum
data.excerpt: In 58 BC Gaius Iulius Caesar obtained the proconsulship of Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul, and in Book VII of his Commentaries on the Gallic War he left a first-hand account of how Celtic hillforts were built and how they were taken. The passage on Avaricum describes the Gallic timber-and-stone wall, the twenty-five days of work on the Roman siege ramp and the massacre of almost all of the town’s roughly forty thousand inhabitants.
data.metaTitle: Caesar on Celtic hillfort walls and the capture of Avaricum
data.metaDescription: How Gaius Iulius Caesar himself described Celtic fortifications (murus gallicus) and the capture of Avaricum during the Gallic wars he began in 58 BC.

timeline.title: The revolt of Vercingetorix
timeline.description: A great revolt of the Gallic tribes broke out under the leadership of Vercingetorix of the Arverni tribe.

timeline.title: The siege and capture of Avaricum
timeline.description: After 25 days of building a siege ramp, Caesar’s legions took the hillfort of Avaricum; its inhabitants were killed.

timeline.title: The siege of Alesia
timeline.description: The fall of Avaricum was followed by the famous siege and capture of Alesia, where Vercingetorix was finally defeated.

children.text: In 58 BC Gaius Iulius Caesar, one of the most brilliant commanders and politicians in the history of mankind, obtained the proconsulship of both Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul. He thus had open ground on which to put his extraordinary gifts as a commander and his political ambitions into practice. Southern Gaul was largely pacified and had been a Roman province for almost a century, but the distant parts of what is today northern France, Belgium and Switzerland attracted his ambitious nature. He began campaigning at once and in the following years defeated the Helvetii, the Sequani, the Nervii, the Menapii and the Treveri on the Rhine, as well as the Senones and the Carnutes. It was hard to find a tribe, apart from the Aedui, that had not risen at least once against his legions of occupation. Every year it seemed that he had pacified all the tribes, and every autumn a revolt flared up at another end of Gaul. Instability in Gaul forced him to return from his expedition to Britain in 55 BC, as it did again in 54 BC. The campaign of the year 52 was indisputably the hardest, the most complicated and the most decisive.

children.text: The revolt gained a great resonance when the wealthiest Gallic tribe, the Arverni, joined it. From this tribe came Caesar’s opponent, the Gallic leader Vercingetorix. He became the leader of all the Gauls and went over to the attack most resolutely. Caesar, however, did not lag behind and launched a counter-offensive. First he took the town of Cenabum, which was among the centres of the revolt. Then he crossed the Loire and set out for the territory of the Bituriges. It was at the town of Noviodunum that the armies of Caesar and Vercingetorix met for the first time. In that fight Caesar’s cavalry, reinforced by Germanic horsemen, defeated the Gallic cavalry. The Gauls decided to change their tactics and not to engage in frontal battles. Next came the capture of the hillfort of Avaricum, whose inhabitants were killed. After the destruction of Avaricum there followed one of the most famous sieges of a town (or rather a hillfort) in the whole of antiquity – the siege and capture of Alesia. A great deal has been written about that siege – for example on the valka.cz website.

children.text: The quotation from the work of Iulius Caesar himself (Commentaries on the Gallic War) that I give below concerns the capture of the Avaricum just mentioned. This exceptional work, which only confirms Caesar’s genius and versatility, was created by Caesar directly in the course of the campaign: amid countless duties of command he dictated the events of the preceding days to a scribe. His matter-of-fact, spare and yet highly gripping style can hold the reader even after more than 2,000 years. The passage on the capture and destruction of the town/hillfort of Avaricum is very interesting for the focus of our website, because in it the commander Caesar describes, from the conqueror’s point of view, the construction and use of Celtic hillforts, and above all brings the reader close to the course of a siege and the capture of a hillfort – a story that in various forms was played out countless times in the territory of present-day Slovakia as well, except that we can usually read it only from archaeological excavations and almost never have such detailed “first-hand” accounts as we do in the case of Caesar’s work.

blocks.text:
At the common council (of the Gauls, who had earlier risen against Roman rule under the very able commander Vercingetorix – note by Orgoň) Avaricum too was discussed: whether they should set fire to it or defend it. The Bituriges threw themselves at the feet of all the Gauls present, begging them not to force them to burn with their own hands the most beautiful town of perhaps the whole of Gaul, which was both the protection and the ornament of their tribe. They said they would easily defend it because of its natural position, for it was surrounded by a river and a marsh and had only a single, very narrow approach. Their request was granted, although Vercingetorix was at first against it, but then agreed under the influence of their pleading and the sympathy of all those present. They chose defenders fit to defend the town.
16/ Vercingetorix set off slowly after Caesar and chose for his camp a place protected by marshes and thickets, sixteen miles from Avaricum. There he had himself informed regularly by his trusted scouting patrols of everything that was being done at Avaricum, and accordingly gave orders as to what was to be done. He lay in wait for all our detachments that went out to gather fodder and grain, and when they had to go a good distance from the camp, he attacked them group by group and did them damage; although our men, as far as could be reckoned, guarded against this by not going out at the same time nor by the same road.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII

blocks.text:
17/ Caesar placed his camp beside that part of the town where the approach was narrow and free of the river and the marsh, as we have already noted, and began to prepare a siege ramp, to move up protective sheds and to build two siege towers. The natural position did not allow the town to be surrounded with a ramp all the way round. He kept urging the Boii and the Aedui without respite to supply grain. The Aedui gave him little support and showed no effort at all. And the Boii, who had no great stores because they were a small and weak tribe, quickly used up themselves what they had.
Although our army suffered terrible shortages of supply because of the poverty of the Boii, the unwillingness of the Aedui and the burning of isolated farmsteads – and to such an extent that the soldiers had been without food for several days and eased their terrible hunger only by driving in livestock from distant villages – not a word was heard unworthy of the dignity of the Roman nation and of their previous victories. Indeed, when Caesar addressed the individual legions at the siege works and said that he would break off the siege of the town if it was too hard for them to bear the want, all the soldiers begged him not to do it. For years, they said, they had suffered no disgrace under his command and had never left any place without success. If he were to abandon the siege he had begun, they would regard it as their own disgrace. It was better, they said, to endure every hardship than to leave unavenged the Roman citizens who had fallen victim to Gallic treachery at Cenabum. They put the same demands to the centurions and the military tribunes, who were to convey them to Caesar.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII

blocks.text:
18/ When the siege towers had come close to the walls of the town, Caesar learned from prisoners that Vercingetorix had set out nearer to Avaricum because his fodder had run out, and that he had himself gone off with the cavalry and the light infantry, which was accustomed to fighting among horsemen, to lie in ambush at the place where, as he supposed, our soldiers would come for fodder the next day.
After this news Caesar set out quietly with the army at midnight and by morning was already at the enemy camp. The enemy quickly learned of Caesar’s arrival from their scouting patrols. They withdrew their wagons and baggage into denser woodland and with all their fighting forces took up battle positions on a bare hillock. As soon as Caesar received a report of this, he at once ordered the personal baggage to be put quickly in one place and the men to be ready for battle.
19/ The little hill sloped gently. On almost every side it was surrounded by a marsh, hard to cross and impassable, which was no wider than fifty feet. On this hillock the Gauls held their ground, relying on its natural position. They had already torn down the little bridges beforehand and, tribe by tribe, guarded all the fords and crossings over the marsh. They were determined to attack the Romans from above if the Romans tried to force a way across.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII

blocks.text:
Anyone who looked only at how immediately close the enemies were to one another would think that the Gauls were willing to join battle on almost equal terms; but anyone who properly noted the unequal situation of the two sides would realise that all the courage of the Gauls was nothing but empty boasting.
 
 
The soldiers were indignant that, although so small a distance separated them, the enemy could still bear the sight of them, and they most urgently asked Caesar to give the signal for battle. But Caesar explained to them how many losses and how many lives of brave men they would pay for the victory. Seeing, he said, the determination with which they would throw themselves into any danger for his glory, he would have to condemn himself as utterly unjust if he did not value their lives more highly than his own glory. In this way he calmed the soldiers and led them back to camp that same day, and set about making further arrangements connected with the siege of the town.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII

blocks.alt: Gaius Iulius Caesar: Konštrukcia keltských hradísk a dobývanie Avarica

blocks.text:
20/ When Vercingetorix returned to his soldiers, they accused him of treason, because, they said, he had moved the camp nearer to the Romans, because he had gone off himself with the whole cavalry, because he had left such great fighting forces without a commander, and because the Romans had exploited his departure most advantageously and most swiftly. All this, they said, could not have happened by chance or without a plan. He preferred, they said, to hold the rule over Gaul by Caesar’s favour rather than as an expression of their own recognition.
To that accusation Vercingetorix replied:
As for his moving the camp, that had happened because of the lack of fodder, and moreover they themselves had urged him to it. And as for his advancing nearer to the Romans, he had been moved to it by the natural position of a place that defends itself even without artificial fortification. In marshy terrain the cavalry was not needed, whereas there, where the horsemen had gone off with him, their service was useful. When he left, he had deliberately handed over the supreme command to no one, so that his deputy should not be carried away by the impatience of the men, for he saw that all of them were eager out of love of comfort, since they no longer wished to endure the hard conditions of war. Whether the Romans had appeared by chance or had come on someone’s information, the Gauls must be grateful to fortune alone that they had had the chance to see from above both the insignificant size of the Roman army and to look with contempt upon the valour of those who had not dared to join battle and had withdrawn back to their camp in disgrace. He had, he said, no desire at all for rule from Caesar’s hands by means of treachery, when he could attain it by a victory which, he said, was already certain both for him and for all the Gauls. Indeed, he would even hand the supreme command back to them if they were convinced that it was rather they who were doing him honour than he them by fighting for their survival.
“So that you may understand that I am speaking sincerely,” he said, “listen to the Roman soldiers.” He had the slaves brought forward whom he had seized a few days earlier while they were gathering fodder, whom he had tormented with hunger and kept imprisoned. They had been instructed in advance how to answer the questions. They therefore said that they were soldiers of the Roman legions. Out of hunger and want, they said, they had secretly left the camp to see whether a little grain or some head of livestock might be found in the countryside. The whole army, they said, suffered the same want; no one, they said, had strength left and no one, they said, was any longer able to endure the labour of fortification. For that reason, they said, the commander-in-chief had decided to lead the army away in three days’ time if he did not succeed in taking the town.
“These are the good services,” said Vercingetorix, “that I have performed for you, and now you accuse me of treason. I, without a drop of your blood, have almost starved to death a mighty army that was accustomed to victory. I have seen to it that no Gallic tribe will receive this army on its territory in its shameful flight.”
21/ The whole assembly expressed its agreement by shouting and, as was their custom, clashed their weapons, which the Gauls did when they approved someone’s speech. Vercingetorix, they said, was an excellent commander, there was no need to doubt his reliability, and this war could not be waged more sensibly. They decided that ten thousand men chosen from the whole army should be sent to help the town of Avaricum. They took the view that the common survival should not be left to the Bituriges alone, for they were aware that if the Bituriges held that town, the fruits of victory would also fall into their hands. 
 
 22/ By the unique efforts of our soldiers all sorts of countermeasures of the Gauls were thwarted, for they are very ingenious and very capable of imitating and carrying out everything that someone explains to them. They know how to defend themselves with rope nooses against siege hooks: once they have caught them fast, they at once haul them up on a winch inside over the walls; they know how to undermine ramps, and all the more skilfully because they have great iron-ore mines among them and because they know and use every kind of gallery. And the whole curtain wall they fitted on all sides with multi-storey towers, and these they covered with hides. In frequent sorties by day and by night they threw fire onto the ramp and attacked our soldiers at the siege works. The height of our towers, which rose continuously as the ramp was raised, they matched by lengthening their own towers. The progress of our open mines towards the walls they hindered with charred and sharpened beams, hot pitch and very heavy boulders, and in this way prevented our men from approaching the walls.
23/ All Gallic walls look roughly like this: beams are laid on the ground at right angles, continuously along the whole length, with equal gaps, namely two feet apart. These are then joined together on the inside and properly packed with earth. The gaps just mentioned are filled at the front with large stones. Once the beams have been laid and firmly joined, a further layer is placed on top, in such a way that exactly the same gap is kept between the beams, except that the upper beam does not lie on the lower one, but the individual beams are held firmly in place by stones inserted one by one between them. In this way the whole structure is built up gradually until the required height of the wall is reached.
Such a construction of a wall not only looks very handsome and varied, because beams and stones alternate in regular straight rows, but it is also a very suitable and effective defence for towns, since the stone protects against fire and the timber structure, in turn, against the blows of the ram; that structure is bound on the inside of the work with continuously jointed beams mostly forty feet long and can neither be broken through nor torn apart. 
24/ Although many obstacles made the siege impossible and our soldiers were held back in their work the whole time by cold and incessant downpours, they nevertheless worked without a break, and in this way overcame every obstacle and in twenty-five days built a siege ramp three hundred and thirty feet wide and eighty feet high. When the ramp was almost touching the enemy wall and Caesar, as was his habit, was spending the night at the works and encouraging the soldiers not to stop working even for a moment, shortly before midnight smoke could be seen rising from the ramp, which the enemy had set alight from a mine. At the same time a shout went up along the whole length of the walls and the enemy made a sortie through two gates on both flanks of the towers. Others again, from the length of the walls, threw burning torches and dry wood onto the ramp, poured on boiling pitch and other inflammable material, so that there was not even time to think where help or action was needed first. But by Caesar’s order two legions were always on standby in front of the camp, and even more of them were taking turns in shifts at the works; some quickly put up resistance to the sorties, others pulled the towers back and dug cut-off trenches in the ramp, and literally everyone ran out of the camp to put out the fire.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII

blocks.text:
25/ Although the night had already passed, fighting was still going on everywhere and the enemy still did not lose hope of victory, all the more so because they saw the burnt sheds of our towers and observed that our unprotected soldiers were having difficulty coming to help, while they themselves were sending fresh forces in place of the exhausted and were aware that the whole survival of Gaul depended on that moment. And in this situation something memorable took place before our eyes which, in our opinion, must not go unnoticed.
A certain Gaul in front of the gate of the town was throwing into the fire, against our siege tower, lumps of tallow and pitch which others were handing into his hands. He was struck in the right side by a missile from a war engine and fell dead. As he lay on the ground, one of the nearest soldiers simply stepped over him and carried on with the same work. When a missile from a war engine killed him too, a third at once took the place of the second, and a fourth the place of the third. And the defenders did not leave that place empty until they had put out the fire on the ramp, until they had pushed the enemy back from every sector and until the fighting was over.
26/ Since everything the Gauls attempted had no success at all, they decided to flee from the town the next day. Vercingetorix first urged them to it and then ordered it outright. They hoped that the men would not suffer great losses if they attempted it in the silence of the night, for Vercingetorix’s camp was not far from the town and the continuous marsh stretching between the town and the camp would hold the Romans back from pursuit.
When they were preparing to leave in the night, the mothers of the households suddenly ran out into the streets, threw themselves weeping at the feet of their husbands and begged them most earnestly not to hand them and their common children over to the enemy to be killed, since they were weak by nature and so could not take flight with them. When they saw that the men were insisting on their intention – in the greatest danger fear usually knows no pity – the women set up a cry and so betrayed the flight to the Romans. At that the Gauls, afraid that the Roman cavalry would occupy the roads in advance, gave up this intention.
27/ The next day Caesar had the tower moved forward again and completed the siege works he had ordered earlier. Just then a great downpour came on, and Caesar realised that this was very suitable weather for carrying out his plan, for he saw that the guards on the walls were not so carefully posted. He therefore ordered his soldiers to slow down the work on the siege works and explained his intention to them. He secretly made the legions ready for battle in covered trenches and encouraged them finally to reap the harvest of victory for so much toil. He also announced that he would reward those who were the first to get onto the walls, and then gave the soldiers the signal to attack. At that the soldiers poured out and quickly filled the walls.
28/ The enemy, surprised by the attack and driven from the walls and the towers, took up a wedge formation in the market square and in the more open spaces, firmly determined to fight a decisive battle in formation if they were attacked from any side. As soon as they saw that no one was coming down from the fortifications onto the level ground, but that the whole length of the walls all around was merely filling up, they threw away their weapons in fear that in the end they would not even be able to get out, and ran headlong into the most remote parts of the town. Some of them were cut down there by the soldiers as they crowded in the narrow gates, and some were cut down by the horsemen after they had come out of the gates. None of our men went after booty. The slaughter at Cenabum and the toilsome labour on the siege works had aroused such anger in them that they spared neither old men, nor women, nor infants.
In the end, out of a total of about forty thousand people, barely eight hundred reached Vercingetorix alive and unharmed, namely those who had run out of the town at the very first shout. He received them late at night in silence, as soon as they came running in. Afraid that their arrival and the pity of the ordinary soldiers would cause an uproar in the camp, he ordered his confidants and the chiefs of the tribes, posted along the road, to divide them up and lead them away to their own countrymen, to that part of the camp which had been allotted to each tribe at the beginning.
29/ The next day Vercingetorix called an assembly at which he consoled and encouraged the Gauls not to lose heart altogether and not to grieve too much over the misfortune that had befallen them. The Romans, he said, had not won by valour, nor in open battle, but by an unusual readiness and skill in siege warfare, in which the Gauls had no experience. Whoever expects nothing but successes in war is mistaken. He had had no intention whatever of defending Avaricum, as they themselves could testify. It was only the folly of the Bituriges and the excessive indulgence of the rest, he said, that was the cause of this misfortune.
blocks.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar
blocks.source: Commentaries on the Gallic War (De Bello Gallico), Book VII
